runs.text: vida, ou eſtado, & fim de cadahum.

lines.note: Continues the preceding page's account of a person's life, condition, and end. The printed cadahum remains a single word; this is ordinary running text rather than a heading.
Tenmon is the gate of the royal palace. The damaged Portuguese still supports Porta and Rey, correcting the OCR's missing letters without changing paços or the historical del construction.
Tennai is explained by ten no uchi, within heaven. The gloss prints ao ceo; it is retained rather than regularized to a different Portuguese preposition.
Tennen describes what occurs naturally or a natural thing. The initial vowel of Naturalmente is a, as supported by both the visible type and the following natural.
Tennho is explained as a woman of heaven and equated with Quengio, a woman of elevated court rank. The Portuguese Mo- begins Molher on the next row; the Japanese spellings are not modernized.

runs.text: lher de grande dignidade que ſerue em caſa do

lines.note: Completes Molher and describes a woman of high rank serving in the imperial household. The continuous dignidade and the long s of ſerue correct spurious OCR spacing and f.

Dairi completes the imperial-household sense, after which the entry also gives a celestial woman. Dairi is a Japanese title embedded in Portuguese; the damaged type is read as Dairi, without the OCR's extra r.
Tennin, explained as ten no hito, is a celestial person or angel. The final headword letters support nin rather than OCR no; the gloss divides celestial across the following physical line.
Lestial completes celestial in the preceding angel or heavenly-person gloss. The short continuation remains an independent physical row.

runs.text: Ouuir todas as couſas do mundo.

lines.note: Tennitsuu is the ability to hear all things in the world, conventionally heavenly hearing. Ouuir is printed continuously, and mundo corrects the OCR's murdo.
Ten no toku is the benefit or bounty of heaven. The Portuguese abbreviation Bẽs is kept unexpanded, and the following example explains the encompassing character of this benefit.

The example describes heaven's covering all things with nothing outside it as its virtue. Vouotte and the attached naqiua are retained as printed; the Portuguese explanation begins with O and continues below.

runs.text: estar tudo de baixo do ceo, & ſujeito às ſuas

lines.note: The Portuguese explains everything as being beneath heaven and subject to its influences. The infinitive estar has a visible final r, correcting OCR esta; the provisional short-s rendering of the st type is retained.

runs.text: influencias, eße he o bem, & proueito, que ſe re-

lines.note: Influencias completes the preceding possessive phrase, and the rest identifies that condition as heaven's benefit. The middle letters support influencias rather than the garbled OCR inflitentias; re- continues recebe below.
Cebe completes recebe, receiving the benefit from heaven. This closes the explanation of ten no toku rather than beginning the next hand-related entry.

The gloss identifies the back of the hand, corresponding to te no koo. The headword visibly retains the draft's doubled n in Tenno; the extra letter is not silently removed to match the expected Japanese phrase.

The entry gives Teno fura, then prefers te no ura with Latin potiùs; both refer to the palm of the hand. The abraded first vowel is retained as u after comparison with the final a and vra. NINJAL identifies te no hara (fara), so this local vowel remains a nonblocking uncertainty. Lexical aid: NINJAL, Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, version 202510, record 255a09, CC BY 4.0 (https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html).

Te no joo wo tsukusu is illustrated as doing something with all one’s effort and exactness. Both giǒ marks are downward carons; the Portuguese Fa continues zer below without a securely visible terminal hyphen.

runs.text: zer algũa couſa cõ todas as forças, & exacção.

lines.note: Completes Fazer and gives the manner of performance: with all one’s strength and exactness. The abbreviating tilde in cõ and the historical spelling exacção are retained.

runs.text: Toalha de alimpar as mãos, ou o rosto.

lines.note: Tenogoi is a towel for wiping the hands or face. The printed form is retained rather than modernized to tenugui, and alimpar remains the historical Portuguese verb.

runs.text: Oução. Poſto que não he palaura

lines.note: Te no mushi is glossed as oução, a mite or itch-causing creature. The final rounded type in Oução is read as o rather than OCR s; the following qualification says that this Japanese expression is not current.

Completes the warning that the expression is not current, then gives mushi as the more appropriate term. Muxi is embedded in this Portuguese usage explanation, with the alternative continued on the next row.

Latin l introduces tsubomushi as the alternative to mushi; Vide supra refers the reader to the earlier entries. This continuation belongs to the Portuguese usage note and does not establish a new headword.
Te no ura denotes the palm. The first example begins the phrase for turning one’s hand over, with the object particle continuing on the next row after the printed break.
The object particle and kaesu complete te no ura wo kaesu, turning the hand. A second example repeats the phrase; its initial letter is T rather than OCR F.
The full comparison describes a person who changes as easily as turning the palm. Cauaru is kawaru, to change; the clear a after c corrects OCR ciuaru, while fitogia supplies hito ja.

runs.text: homem que ſe muda, & vira tam facilmente

lines.note: The Portuguese calls him a man who changes and turns so easily. Facilmente has the ordinary m-n sequence visible in the scan, rather than OCR facilmemte.

runs.text: como quem vira a palma da mão.

lines.note: Completes the comparison with someone turning over the palm of the hand. The continuous como corrects the OCR’s spurious internal letters and space.
Tenpai is equated with taore, taoreru, falling. The printed Portuguese infinitive is Cair, with its final r restored; the upright S marks written usage.
This separate homophonous Tenpai denotes the king’s cup or goblet. The n in the headword corrects OCR Teupai; it is distinguished from the preceding falling sense by its complete new gloss.
Tenpan, explained as soe-meshi, is additional rice beyond a regular portion. The faint paired terminal strokes are retained as a line-break hyphen, and acre- continues centa below.

runs.text: centa de mais alem da regra, ou porção ordina-

lines.note: Completes acrecenta: rice added beyond the rule or ordinary portion. The printed porção and ordina- are retained, with the latter completed on the next physical row.

Completes ordinaria and locates this extra rice in the kitchens of Zen religious communities. Ienxùs is the Japanese sect name embedded in the Portuguese sentence; its grave mark and Portuguese plural s remain as printed.

runs.text: Tenpi. i, Tenno fi. l, tenqua.

lines.note: Tenpi is heavenly fire, explained as ten no hi and alternatively tenkwa. The separated fi. l, is a Japanese noun followed by the Latin alternative marker, not the OCR’s malformed fial.
Tenpo means supplementing or replenishing, explained by soe oginou. The abraded headword supports Tenpo rather than renoo; the Portuguese begins replenishing and increasing, continued below.
Completes acrecentar and gives strength as something that can be replenished or increased. The upright S is the written-usage label, separate from the italic Portuguese explanation.

runs.text: Frauta, q̃ tangem os que andão per

lines.note: Tenpuku is a flute played by people travelling around to beg. The Portuguese verb has the descender of g in tangem, not the OCR’s z, and q̃ is retained without expansion.

runs.text: diuerſas partes pedindo eſmola pollas portas.

lines.note: Continues the flute description: the players visit different places asking for alms at doors. The historical pollas and the printed long-s forms are retained.
Tenpuku wo fuku means blowing or playing this flute. The object-particle sequence uuo corrects OCR unro, while the visible g in Tanger corrects Tanoer.
Tenqe is explained as heaven’s flowers, glossed as roses or fulas that fall. The unusual printed fulas remains unchanged rather than being silently replaced by flores; caẽ abbreviates the verb.

runs.text: do ceo, como dizem os Bonzos que cahião quã-

lines.note: Continues the Buddhist account of flowers falling from heaven. Cahião has the open lower curl of italic h, matching homem on c1-l027, rather than the closed bowl of b; this supports correcting OCR cabião. Quã- continues quando below.
Completes quando and identifies Shaka, the Buddha, as the preacher. Xaca is the Japanese name embedded in the Portuguese clause; the grave mark in prègaua is retained.
Tenken is explained by shirushi, shirusu, recording or noting something. The initial T is one letter, not the OCR’s TF; a- begins apontar on the next row.

runs.text: pontar cantidade, ou numero dalgũa couſa co-

lines.note: Completes apontar and specifies recording the quantity or number of a thing. The historical cantidade and dalgũa remain, and co- begins the comparison continued below.

runs.text: mo quem faz rol de quanto tem, ou empreſtoa,

lines.note: Completes como and compares the action to listing how much one possesses or lends. Empreſtoa is retained as the visibly printed historical form.
Closes the inventory-making explanation with tenken suru, to perform such recording. Vt is italic apparatus, whereas the Japanese example is upright.
Tenki is explained by sora no ki and defined as the weather or its quality. The definition runs into the top of the second column; the final ampersand is body text and is fully included in the crop.

runs.text: maneira do tempo como quandoſe diz, faz bõ

lines.note: Continues the tenki definition from the preceding column: the character of the weather, as when one says it is good. The malformed quaondoſe is corrected to quandoſe; the close printed joining before ſe is retained.
Completes the contrast between good and bad weather, then begins tenki ga nodoyakana, describing tranquil weather. The adjectival ending is divided across this row and the next.
Na completes nodoyacana; the gloss states that the weather is serene. The initial na is Japanese continuation text, not a separate headword.
Tenqua is here explained by matoi tsutsumu, wrapping or enveloping oneself. The final vowel of tçutçumu is read as u, while the historical Portuguese emburulharſe is preserved.

runs.text: ou encobrirſe como faz o bicho de ſeda meten-

lines.note: The comparison is with the silkworm concealing itself. Meten- begins the reflexive participial expression completed on the next row.
Completes metendoſe: the silkworm puts itself inside its enclosing sheath or cocoon. Folhelho is kept as the printed Portuguese word rather than replaced by a modern technical term.
This distinct Tenqua entry means heavenly fire, explained as ten no hi. Both the explanatory Tenno and the example’s divided Ten- correct OCR Tonno and Ton-.
Tenqua furicudaru describes fire descending from heaven. Decer preserves the historical spelling without an inserted s; the damaged final vowel in fogo is read as o rather than OCR e.
Tenkafun is identified only as a particular medicine. The gloss does not itself justify supplying a modern plant or chemical identification.
Tenkoo, explained by ten no hikari, denotes heaven’s brightness. The weak l in Claridade is supported by the surviving narrow type and the light gloss; S is an upright written-usage label.
Tenryo is the sovereign’s judgment or consideration, explained by teioo no omonbakari. The Portuguese begins with knowledge and continues with prudence on the next line.
Completes the royal-judgment gloss as the king’s prudence. The printed u in prudencia corrects OCR pradencia without altering the historical capitalization of Rey.

runs.text: Ley, ou ordem com que ſe gouerna o

lines.note: Tenri is the law or ordering by which the world is governed. The small e is visible in Ley; OCR Ly had omitted it.

runs.text: mundo: ou razão, & ordem que ſe não ve cõ

lines.note: Completes the governing of the world and gives a second formulation: reason and order not seen with the eyes. The unaccented ve and abbreviated cõ remain as printed.
Os olhos completes the statement that heavenly order is invisible to the eyes. This brief continuation closes Tenri before the following headword.
Tensai is heaven’s knowledge. The example contrasts human knowledge, ninchi, with heavenly knowledge and begins a construction whose negative predicate continues below.

runs.text: Não ſe pode ſaber por ſciẽ-

lines.note: Completes the Japanese negative comparison, saying that even human or heavenly knowledge does not reach it. The Portuguese explains that it cannot be known by science or knowledge; ſciẽ- continues below.
Completes the contrast between human and celestial knowledge. The printed celestial is retained without changing the provisional st-ligature expansion.

runs.text: Prohibição, ou mandado por eſcrito a

lines.note: Tensat denotes a written prohibition or posted order. The final bare t is the Sino-Japanese checked ending, supported by the repeated Tenſatuo below; OCR Tenfar misread both s and the final type.

runs.text: cerca das ſearas dos campos, ou varzeas pera

lines.note: The order concerns crops in fields or low-lying cultivated land. Das and campos replace OCR dae and campor; the printed varzeas is retained without a supplied modern accent.

runs.text: que ſe não ſeguem, ou laurem por algũa cauſa.

lines.note: Completes the prohibition against reaping or ploughing for some reason. Laurem visibly contains the historical consonantal u after a, restoring a letter omitted in OCR larem.
Tensat wo orosu means issuing or posting the written prohibition. The Portuguese begins placing this law or prohibition; pro continues on the next row with no secure terminal hyphen.
Completes prohibição and specifies writing it on a board. The printed taboa and the abbreviated vowel in nalgũa are preserved.
Tensoo is the office or duty of presenting communications to the sovereign, explained by soomon no yaku. The definition’s verb is completed by recado on the following row.
Completes the office’s function: giving a message or speaking to the king. This explains the preceding Japanese official title rather than opening a new entry.

runs.text: Palaura que corre na igreja por Deos,

lines.note: Tenson is described as a word used in the church for God. This is the dictionary’s own statement about Christian usage, not a claim about all Japanese senses of the term.
Gives lord of heaven as the alternative explanation of the church’s use of Tenson. The short row completes the preceding headword.

runs.text: Freſta como trapeira do telhado que ſ

lines.note: Tensu is a roof opening like a dormer or skylight. The final long s abuts the right rule; an expected following e in ſe is not distinctly legible, so the supplied fragment ſ is retained with this nonblocking caveat.
Completes the roof-opening description: it lowers and raises. The visible a after b corrects OCR abuixa; aleuanta retains the historical u/v spelling.

runs.text: Agoa, ou chuua do ceo. Mas cõmun-

lines.note: Tensui first means water or rain from heaven. The gloss then begins a more common usage, with cõmun- continued on the next physical row.

runs.text: mente ſe toma per tina, ou balde que poem ſo-

lines.note: Completes commonly and says the term is taken as a tub or bucket placed overhead. The damaged m of toma is read from its surviving strokes. Per is chosen from the middle vowel’s open right side and inner stroke, unlike the closed o in nearby por; the vowel remains a nonblocking caveat. The terminal mark after ſo is visible before bre below.

runs.text: bre os telhados, ou noutra parte pera receber

lines.note: Completes sobre and places the receptacle on roofs or elsewhere to receive rainwater. Receber has e in its middle syllable, correcting OCR recaber.

runs.text: agoa da chuua pera contra o fogo. Vt,

lines.note: Specifies rainwater stored as protection against fire. The example begins tensui wo oku, placing such a water vessel, with the headword divided after Ten-.
Completes tensui wo oku and translates it as putting this tub in place. Voqu represents oku; the object particle remains attached in the diplomatic text.
Tentaku is explained as heaven’s message or pronouncement, ten no go-tsuge. The Portuguese calls it revelation, with the final letters tight against the right rule.

runs.text: do ceo, ou de Deos. ¶ Item, Influencias

lines.note: Completes revelation from heaven or God, then opens another sense involving heavenly influences. The printed distinction between the two explanations is preserved.

runs.text: do ceo, ou beneficios, & merces que Deos faz.

lines.note: Completes the alternative sense: heavenly influences, benefits, and favours bestowed by God. This is the dictionary’s Portuguese explanatory framing.
Tentsuu is explained by ten ni tsuuzuru, communicating with or reaching heaven. Both length marks over u are kept as carons according to their visible shape.

runs.text: com o ceo, ou chegar tè o ceo.

lines.note: Completes the definition as communicating with heaven or reaching as far as heaven. The g in chegar corrects OCR chezar; the upright S marks written usage.
Tentei is explained as heaven’s sovereign and glossed first as king, then as God. The abbreviating tildes in Tẽno and Itẽ are preserved rather than expanded.

runs.text: Inimigo de Deos, ou do ceo.

lines.note: Tenteki is an enemy of God or heaven. The concise Portuguese gloss supplies both alternatives without a Japanese example.
Tentoo is explained as heaven’s way, ten no michi. The gloss begins the way or order of heaven, and the headword’s mark remains a downward caron.
Adds the providence of heaven, then begins the statement that the authors commonly call God by this name. The printed doubled consonants in Commummente and the line-end chama- remain.

runs.text: mos ja a Deos por eſte nome. Poſtoque os ge-

lines.note: Completes chamamos and the authors’ use of this name for God. Ge- begins their contrast with non-Christian usage; the following tios lacks the expected n of gentios, and no letter is silently supplied.

runs.text: tios não parece que atinauão mais que com o

lines.note: Continues the statement that the non-Christian speakers appeared to apprehend only the earlier sense of heavenly order. The physical ge-/tios division is preserved despite its anomalous omitted n.
Completes the contrast by referring back to the first sense of Tentǒ, heaven’s way or providential order. This closes the long entry.

Tentoku is qualified by preferably ten no toku, the blessings or goods of heaven. This repeats the earlier expression with an explicit wording preference; the Latin qualifier is italic and the Japanese forms upright.
